name: Fluency and Reading Supports
title: Fluency and Reading Supports
answer: Fluency and reading supports use speech tools to help students read aloud and access text. For younger readers they can add fluency practice and flag missed or slow words, while for older students they can read text aloud, highlight words, break words into syllables, and define terms so a reading disability does not block grade level content. The idea matters because the same support can either open access or replace needed practice, so teachers and the individualized education program team must decide when it helps.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea covers two related uses of speech technology in reading. For younger readers, a tool listens as a student reads aloud and marks words the student missed or read slowly, giving extra fluency practice. For older students who struggle with print, reading supports such as Microsoft Immersive Reader and Read&Write by Texthelp can read text aloud, highlight words as they are spoken, break words into syllables, and define unfamiliar terms. The problem it solves is access: a student with a reading disability can use these supports to learn science or history at grade level, and without them that student might fall behind in every subject, not just reading. The harder question is when a support helps and when it gets in the way, which the text frames as strategic offloading.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the younger grades, speech tools can provide extra fluency practice by listening to a student read aloud and marking words that were missed or read slowly. Because these tools struggle with young voices, a teacher should listen too. For older students who struggle with print, reading supports can read text aloud, highlight words as they are spoken, break words into syllables, and define unfamiliar terms. A student with a reading disability can then use those supports to learn science or history at grade level. The text does not give separate grade bands beyond younger readers and older students, but it places the decision about when a support applies with the individualized education program team.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports a large study that found strong reading gains from an AI reading platform used by regular teachers, but it notes that the study's authors were connected to the company, so districts should confirm results locally (Srinivasan & Murthy, 2021). It also refers to Chapter 5's point that these tools struggle with young voices, so a teacher should listen too. The text describes strategic offloading as a researcher framing (Seung & Basham, 2026), not as a study finding. The supplied text does not give a formal evidence label for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets several limits. Speech tools struggle with young voices, so a teacher should listen too rather than relying on the tool alone. The study behind the reading platform had authors connected to the company, so districts should confirm results locally. The harder question is when a support helps and when it gets in the way, because in a history lesson text to speech may be exactly right, while in a reading lesson the same support might skip the practice the student most needs. The individualized education program team should decide which applies when, so the decision stays with people.
